Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making eye contact with other people
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette:
Sarah was twenty-six when it happened, though she had not told anyone the full story-not even Mark, her husband, who knew only that something terrible had occurred during the three days she had been missing. She had been leaving her apartment complex late one evening when a man she had met twice at a bar cornered her in the stairwell, a knife at her ribs, and forced her into the back of a van. For the next seventy-two hours he kept her in a windowless basement room, and in that room he controlled every detail of her existence: when she ate, when she slept, whether she was allowed to stand or forced to kneel. His anger was not explosive but constant-a low, simmering fury that leaked into every word he spoke. He watched her without blinking, sometimes for hours, sitting in a chair just beyond her reach, studying her face as if searching for something she could not give. And he used her body in ways that left her feeling scraped hollow, a thing rather than a person. When the police finally found her-an anonymous tip, they said-she was curled on a concrete floor, unable to speak above a whisper.

In the months that followed, Sarah returned to her job as a teller at the downtown branch of First Federal Bank, believing that routine would restore what had been taken. It did not. The first time a customer raised his voice over a misdirected deposit, she felt her chest lock and her vision narrow, and she had to excuse herself to the break room, where she sat shaking for ten minutes. It was not the volume that undid her-the customer had not yelled, only spoken more firmly than usual-but the way his jaw had tightened, the same tightening she had seen in the basement. She began to dread any interaction that carried even a hint of frustration: a colleague sighing over a jammed printer, a manager tapping a pen during a team meeting. Each time, her stomach dropped, and she would look away, fixing her gaze on the floor tiles until the moment passed. She also found herself jumping at the smallest sounds-a door slamming in the bank's lobby, a car backfiring outside, even the sharp click of a cash drawer closing. Her heart would lurch as if the noise were a hand on her shoulder, and she would freeze, scanning the room for a threat that wasn't there. At home, if Mark dropped a spoon in the kitchen or a delivery truck rumbled past the window, she would flinch so hard that she sometimes dropped whatever she was holding.

Eye contact became unbearable. At the bank, she trained herself to look at customers' foreheads or the space just past their shoulders. At home, she turned her face from Mark when he spoke to her in bed, afraid that if she met his eyes he would see something she could not name, or that she would see in his gaze the same patient, appraising stillness she had tried so hard to forget. Intimacy dissolved. When Mark reached for her, her skin crawled with the sense that she was being watched, that she had no control over what was about to happen. She began to lie awake long after he fell asleep, listening to the silence of the apartment, because silence had become its own kind of threat. In the basement, the quiet had always meant something was coming-a new question, a new pain. So she would get up two or three times a night to check the locks on the doors, to peer through the blinds at the empty street, to reassure herself that no one was standing in the dark. But even with the locks checked, she would startle at the creak of the floorboards or the hum of the refrigerator, her whole body tensing as if she were still trapped in that room.

During the day, she found herself replaying the three days in her mind, turning the details over and over as if she might discover a reason for what had happened, a logic that would make it survivable. She would be counting cash at her station and suddenly she was back in the room: the damp smell of concrete, the scrape of the chair legs, the sting of a hand across her cheek. The memories came without warning-a flicker of movement in her peripheral vision, the sound of a key turning in a lock-and when they arrived, they arrived whole, flooding her senses so completely that she had to grip the edge of the counter to keep from falling. The overwhelming emotion left her breathless, and often she would retreat to the bathroom and sit on the closed toilet lid, working to remind herself where she was. Even there, a sudden knock on the stall door could make her gasp and press her hand to her chest.

To quiet the loop of memory, she started spending. Small things at first-a coffee, a lip balm-but then larger purchases: a handbag she did not need, a pair of boots she never wore. The packages arrived at the house, and Mark would raise his eyebrows, but she could not explain that the momentary rush of clicking "buy" was the only time she felt any distance from the basement. The credit card balance crept higher, and with it came a new kind of dread, but she could not stop.

What finally brought Sarah to therapy was not the spending, nor the nights spent checking locks, nor the growing distance between her and Mark. It was a Tuesday afternoon when a young man came to her window to deposit a check. He was polite, soft-spoken, and he looked directly at her as he slid the slip across the counter. She saw his face, young and unthreatening, and for a split second the bank disappeared and she was back on the concrete floor, a pair of eyes fixed on her from a chair. She dropped the deposit slip, excused herself, and walked out of the branch without telling her manager. She drove home in a daze, and that evening she said to Mark, through tears, "I don't know how to live inside my own head anymore." She is here now because she wants to believe that it is possible to feel safe again, though she is not sure what safety would look like, or whether she would recognize it if it came.
